newsitem.title: USA: Baxter operating results higher, expenses cut net income.
newsitem.headline: Baxter operating results higher, expenses cut net income.

text.p: Baxter International Inc. reported higher second-quarter operating results Thursday, but net income fell as the medical products company stepped up spending on research and development and marketing and administration.
Among its research projects, it said it is progressing rapidly on its Nextran xenotransplantation project, which involves development of special animal organs for use as transplants in humans.
Baxter said net income from continuing operations rose 14 percent to $162 million from $142 million in the 1996 period. Operating earnings per share grew 12 percent to 58 cents from 52 cents.
However, the Deerfield, Ill.-based company said its net income fell to $162 million, or 58 cents a share, from $176 million, or 65 cents a share, over the same period.
Sales rose to $1.6 billion from $1.3 billion, led by Baxter's Biotech and IV Systems/Medical Products businesses.

Baxter's Nextran subsidiary is developing genetically engineered pigs with internal organs that may be removed and implanted in humans with end-stage organ failure. As researchers move ahead on it, xenotransplantation is arousing heated debate about its safety, but is viewed by some as a potentially life-saving technology.

"We expect to be in human trials for xenotransplants for either hearts or kidneys by the end of 1998," Baxter President Harry Kraemer said in an interview. "We believe we will be the first company in human clinicals for xenotransplants."
The company's marketing and administrative expenses jumped to $347 million from $282 million, while research and development costs rose to $95 million from $84 million.
Baxter said it expects to grow its 1997 net income in the "low double digits" and exceed its goal of generating at least $300 million in operational cash flow.
Kraemer said Wall Street estimates that the company would generate 1997 sales of about $6.5 billion were "very reasonable."

The company's HemAssist blood substitute product is expected to receive European marketing approval in mid-1998, he said. "Once we have approval in Europe, we would expect a 12- to 18-month period between that and approval in the United States. So ... we would expect approval in the United States (for HemAssist) by the end of 1999," he said.
Baxter's stock rose 44 cents to $57.94 on the New York Stock Exchange in consolidated afternoon trading.
